descriptions: The One Being that the inspired call by many names — Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan (RV 1.164.46); the one bird the poets shape into many (10.114.5); the One that has become all this (8.58.2).
That One which breathed windless by its own power before there was being or non-being, death or immortality, and was born by the power of tapas (RV 10.129.2–3).
The Person who is all this, what was and what will be, lord of immortality; one quarter of him is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven (RV 10.90.2–3).

The highest Brahman whose alone is the light; those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme (AVŚ 10.8.1, 10.7.17); the one-alone god in whom the gods become one (AVŚ 13.4.12–13); 'that is Agni, that the Sun … that is brahman' (VS 32.1).
The self, desireless, wise, immortal, self-existent, lacking nothing; knowing him one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).
negations: 'Then there was neither non-being nor being' (RV 10.129.1)
'Who really knows? … perhaps he does not know' (RV 10.129.6–7)
'You will not find him who produced these — something else has come between you' (RV 10.82.7)
'He is called neither second nor third …' (AVŚ 13.4.16–18)
relation_to_self: Named in the Saṃhitās as the self of what moves and stands (Sūrya, RV 1.115.1), the self present in the golden city of the body (AVŚ 10.2.32–33), the one god who entered the mind (AVŚ 10.8.28) and the ageless self known by the wise (10.8.44); the seer who first 'does not know what he is' (RV 1.164.37) can also say 'I was Manu and the Sun' (4.26.1).
relation_to_world: Both immanent and exceeding: the One has become all this (RV 8.58.2) and the Person covers the earth and exceeds it by ten fingers, three quarters of him beyond (10.90.1–3); the world is made by sacrifice of the Person, by the All-maker, from the Golden Germ, by tapas, or from Time — accounts the Saṃhitās place side by side.
caveat: The Saṃhitās are a liturgy addressed to many gods, each praised in turn as supreme; the statements of one ultimate are a minority of speculative hymns, and they leave the origin itself in question (10.129.6–7). The ritual tradition's own hermeneutics (Mīmāṃsā) reads the corpus for injunctions and holds the deities to be what the mantras name, positing no single describable ultimate; Yāska records the view that there are three deities (Nirukta 7.5) beside the view that one Self is praised in many ways (7.4); Vaiṣṇava readers take the One as Viṣṇu. The one-truth reading (RV 1.164.46) is used by this ontology only in the interpretation layer.
